concepts.title: Formulating Linear Programming Problems
concepts.definition: Formulation turns a resource-allocation story into a linear programming problem: define decision variables, write the objective function to maximise or minimise as a linear expression in them, and translate every resource restriction and non-negativity requirement into linear constraints.
concepts.key_idea: The two structural features are a linear objective and linear constraints with non-negative variables. Words like 'at most' give <= constraints, 'at least' give >= constraints, and 'exactly' gives equality.
question_patterns: A firm makes {p1} profit per unit of product A and {p2} per unit of product B; formulate the LPP to maximise profit.
Define decision variables and write the objective function for the given situation.
Translate 'the mixture must contain at least {r} units of protein' into a constraint.
Write the complete mathematical formulation of the stated diet problem.
Why must decision variables in an LPP be non-negative in most problems?

concepts.title: Feasible Region Graphical Method
concepts.definition: Each linear constraint shades a half-plane, and the intersection of all half-planes with the non-negative quadrant is the feasible region: the set of all points satisfying every constraint simultaneously. A bounded feasible region is a convex polygon; an unbounded one extends infinitely.
concepts.key_idea: Corner points (vertices) of the feasible region are where two boundary lines intersect, and they are the only candidates for an optimal solution of a bounded LPP. Infeasible constraints leave no common region at all.
question_patterns: Graph the constraints {a}x + {b}y <= {c}, x >= 0, y >= 0 and shade the feasible region.
Find the corner points of the feasible region for the given constraints.
What does an empty feasible region indicate about the constraints?
Distinguish a bounded and an unbounded feasible region.
Why is the feasible region of an LPP always convex?

concepts.title: Corner Point Method for Optimum
concepts.definition: The corner point method evaluates the objective function at every vertex of the feasible region: the largest value is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum. This works because a linear function attains its optimum over a convex polygon at a vertex.
concepts.key_idea: Evaluate z = c1 x + c2 y at each corner and compare; ties mean the whole edge between the tied corners is optimal. If two corners give the same maximum, every point on the joining edge does too.
question_patterns: Maximise z = {c1}x + {c2}y subject to the given constraints using the corner point method.
Evaluate the objective z = {c1}x + {c2}y at the vertex ({x}, {y}).
Find the maximum and minimum values of z at the corner points of the given region.
If two corner points give the same maximum value of z, what is the complete optimal set?
Minimise cost z = {c1}x + {c2}y over the stated feasible region.

concepts.title: Bounded Unbounded and Special Cases
concepts.definition: A bounded feasible region guarantees both a maximum and a minimum of the objective. An unbounded region can leave the maximum open: before declaring no finite maximum, test whether the objective grows without bound along a ray in the region. Special cases include multiple optimal solutions, infeasibility and redundancy of a constraint.
concepts.key_idea: For maximisation on an unbounded region, draw z = c1 x + c2 y = k and push k upward; if some edge of the region is parallel to the level lines and the region extends that way, no maximum exists.
question_patterns: Show that z = {c1}x + {c2}y has no maximum over the given unbounded region.
When does an LPP have infinitely many optimal solutions?
What is an infeasible LPP?
Give an example of a redundant constraint and explain the term.
State the condition under which a minimum is guaranteed even for an unbounded region.

worked_examples.q: Maximise z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y <= 4, x, y >= 0.
worked_examples.a: The feasible region is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4). z at (0,0) = 0; at (4,0) = 12; at (0,4) = 16. The maximum is z = 16 at x = 0, y = 4: put everything into the product with the higher unit profit when only the shared resource binds.

worked_examples.q: A corner-point comparison gives z = 20 at (2, 5) and z = 20 at (6, 2). State the optimal set.
worked_examples.a: Since the two vertices give the same objective value and the objective is linear, every point on the edge joining (2, 5) and (6, 2) attains z = 20; the optimal set is that whole edge, not just the two corners.
